ext.title: Mapping the Ideological Marketplace
ext.venue: SSRN working paper, draft dated June 25, 2013 (SSRN 2148801). The text names no journal; its replication link is a Dataverse "ajps" page, which suggests an AJPS submission but does not state one.
ext.document_type: Working paper (SSRN draft) with supplemental materials
ext.coverage: Read the full text file (33,059 lines) in chunks: main text PDF pp.1-42 including references, and supplemental materials from about PDF p.43 to the end, including the supplement's reference list. Figure and table glyph lines (axis ticks, single-letter legend codes, state abbreviations) were filtered out with awk; every figure caption and every word-bearing table was read. All 93 annotation items were read. Page numbers are PDF pages, matching the annotation numbering; printed page = PDF page minus 1. Supplement PDF pages are approximate unless anchored by an annotation.
ext.research_question: How can ideal points be estimated for candidates and contributors across federal and state elections, for incumbents and non-incumbents, from campaign contribution records? Secondary: whether ideology or strategic motives (investor, partisan-electoral) drive contributions, and whether the resulting common-space CFscores are valid and stable enough for work on polarization, state politics, candidate positioning and donor ideology.
ext.theory: Spatial model of giving (PDF pp.6-7, Eq. 1): contributor i allocates amounts y_j across recipients to maximize sum of b_i(y_j) - c_i(y_j) - y_j(delta_j - theta_i)^2, subject to y_j below the legal limit clim_j. Competing accounts tested: the investor model (contributions as payments for access or votes; Denzau and Munger 1986, Snyder 1990), the partisan electoral model (donors fund competitive races to shift party seat share; Wand 2007, 2012), and the ideological model (proximity only). Central claim: individual donors give mainly on ideology, so spatial giving is the appropriate model for individuals and most PACs (PDF pp.22-23).
ext.data: Campaign finance records: over 103 million records, 1979-2012, from 13.4 million individuals and 511,141 organizations to 51,572 candidates and 6,408 committees (PDF p.9; abstract says "over 100 million"). Scaling sample (PDF p.10): 3.93 million individuals plus 261,828 committees and organizations as contributor rows; 13,189 federal candidates, 55,737 state candidates and 9,436 committees as recipient columns. An additional 9.75 million single-recipient donors are projected onto the space as supplementary observations. Inclusion: contributor gave to at least 2 recipients; candidate received from at least 2 contributors; loans and transfers excluded; individual gifts to labor, corporate and trade PACs excluded; corporate and trade PACs excluded from estimation. Unit: contributor-recipient pair; amounts converted to counts of $100 bins capped at 50 ($5,000+). Strategic-giving tests: 5,000 random individuals with at least 25 federal contributions 2004-2012 (N=49,418 for the full 25+ group in the consistency test), 124 labor PACs, 1,312 corporate and trade PACs (PDF pp.18-19). Roll-call comparisons: 96th-112th Congresses. Period-specific estimates require at least 25 contributors per candidate per cycle.
ext.method: Augmented correspondence analysis (CA) on the contributor-by-recipient contingency matrix R (PDF p.7; supplement). Matrix is standardized and decomposed by SVD of K = D_r^(-1/2)(R - rc')D_c^(-1/2); contributor ideal points theta = U D^-1/2 scaled, recipient delta = V D^-1/2. CA is described as nearly equivalent to a log-linear ideal point model (Lowe 2008; ter Braak 1985). Steps: (1) scale federal elections first; (2) scale each state separately, using bridge contributors (those giving to both state and federal races), with an 8-step alternating least-squares routine; (3) jointly re-estimate recipients; (4) normalize so the weighted mean and SD of contribution amounts are 0 and 1. Between-set identification: contributor points are regressed on matched candidate points with an error-in-variables specification (intercept 0.017, slope 0.975, on 29,913 candidates who appear as donors). Presidential nominees get separate pre- and post-nomination scores. Non-incumbent scores: contributor points held fixed; candidate points re-estimated from pre-record contributions. Period-specific CFscores follow Nokken and Poole (2004). Strategic-giving comparison: a right-censored negative binomial count model per donor (IRT-style, adapted from Bonica 2013a), compared by log-likelihood and the Cameron-Windmeijer deviance residual RDev.
ext.identification: Bridging through multi-office donors, not roll calls. 70-90% of contributors who fund state campaigns also give to federal campaigns (PDF p.8), and candidates running for both state and federal office add more bridges. The federal scaling anchors each state's scaling. A final rescaling aligns contributor and candidate distances. Identification is up to a standard normalization. The author argues that the cross-state identification assumption is "unheroic and verifiable": donors have the same ideal point when giving to state and federal candidates (PDF p.24 footnote 13; state-federal correlation 0.88 for all donors, 0.93 for donors to 10+ candidates).
ext.scope: US campaigns, 1979-2012. Candidates for President, Congress, governors, state attorneys general, secretaries of state, other state-wide offices, state legislatures, state supreme courts, federal circuit courts, boards of education and ballot campaigns (PDF p.23, Fig. 2). Also donors, labor, corporate and trade PACs and industry aggregates. Institutions: federal and all 50 states. Claims are about ideology as revealed by giving; no claim about legislative behavior is tested beyond roll-call comparisons.

key_findings.finding: Candidate CFscores correlate with common-space DW-NOMINATE at r = 0.92. Within-party correlations are weaker: House Democrats 0.56, House Republicans 0.66, Senate Democrats 0.64, Senate Republicans 0.72. Figure 1 totals: House incumbents 0.91, open seats 0.93, challengers 0.89; Senate incumbents 0.91, open seats 0.95, challengers 0.92.
key_findings.location: External Validity, PDF p.11 (Fig. 1 on PDF p.13)
key_findings.numbers: r=0.92; within-party House D 0.56 / R 0.66; Senate D 0.64 / R 0.72

key_findings.finding: Non-incumbent CFscores predict future DW-NOMINATE about as well as incumbent CFscores. Incumbent and non-incumbent CFscores correlate highly, and within-party correlations are lower for Democrats.
key_findings.numbers: non-incumbent vs incumbent CFscore r = 0.96 overall, 0.93 R, 0.88 D

key_findings.finding: Roll-call classification: CFscores classify votes nearly as well as roll-call measures, although they never condition on roll calls. Party-only classification is also reported.
key_findings.numbers: House (96th-112th): CFscore 0.880 (APRE 0.638), DW-NOMINATE 0.896 (0.687), Turbo-ADA 0.886 (0.659), party 0.863 (0.588). Senate: CFscore 0.870 (0.607), DW-NOMINATE 0.882 (0.644), party 0.838 (0.514)

key_findings.finding: Period-specific stability: CFscores are more stable across periods than DW-NOMINATE. The text states the result as greater inter-temporal stability.
key_findings.numbers: R2 of static on period-specific: CFscore 0.97 overall, 0.89 D, 0.86 R; DW-NOMINATE House 0.96 (0.86 D, 0.70 R), Senate 0.96 (0.72 D, 0.85 R)

key_findings.finding: Donor-candidate consistency: candidates who also donate have CFscores as contributors that track their CFscores as recipients. The author reads this as both activities expressing the same latent ideology.
key_findings.numbers: r = 0.94 overall, 0.78 D, 0.68 R among 10,406 candidates who gave to at least 5 recipients (of 29,913 candidates who made contributions)

key_findings.finding: Individual donors give on ideology: the ideological model beats both strategic models for individuals. The investor model barely improves on the baseline. Investor model fits better than the ideological model for about 5% of individual donors. For corporate and trade PACs the investor model is competitive with the ideological model, which supports excluding those PACs from estimation.
key_findings.numbers: Log-lik individuals: unrestricted -1,275,233; ideological -1,334,200; partisan -1,405,855; investor -1,504,601; unconstrained investor -1,468,435; baseline -1,520,312. Labor PACs: ideological -231,022; investor -252,936. Corp/trade PACs: ideological -1,694,458; investor -1,695,149; unconstrained investor -1,687,949. RDev for individuals: ideological 0.601, investor 0.412.

key_findings.finding: Strategic allocation is rare among active donors: nearly all donors with 25+ contributions are ideological in the money-weighted SD test.
key_findings.numbers: Only 167 of 49,418 (0.3%) individuals exceed the 0.577 random-giving benchmark; mean money-weighted SD 0.20

key_findings.finding: Sensitivity to strategic covariates is small. Incumbency, majority-party status and competitive seats shift candidate CFscores only at the margins, and DW-NOMINATE is more sensitive to the same covariates.
key_findings.numbers: Largest shifts 0.03-0.05 (about 1/20 of a candidate CFscore SD, about a dozen ranks). Within-party R2 House Republicans 0.698 to 0.751 with covariates (DW-NOMINATE); CFscore static model already explains nearly all variance

key_findings.finding: Congressional polarization differs by measure. CFscores start less polarized and keep growing after 1996, while DW-NOMINATE flattens. Two measures converge by the 112th Congress. Asymmetry also differs: DW-NOMINATE says Republicans moved further than Democrats; CFscores show a near reversal.
key_findings.numbers: Since 1980: DW-NOMINATE mean Democrat 0.20 SD left, mean Republican 0.44 SD right; CFscores mean Democrat 0.50 SD left, mean Republican 0.31 SD right

key_findings.finding: State chamber medians from CFscores match NPAT-based common-space scores closely. Party medians match less well.
key_findings.numbers: 2000-2010 chamber medians r = 0.86 upper, 0.83 lower; party medians r = 0.59 and 0.64 (Republicans), 0.53 and 0.61 (Democrats)

key_findings.finding: State-wide officials are more polarized than legislators. Mean Democrat-Republican distances exceed the congressional party gap for secretaries of state.
key_findings.numbers: Governors 1.48, attorneys general 1.57, secretaries of state 1.81; congressional party distance at the time 1.66; 33 governors, 35 AGs and 35 SoS locate at the extremes of the state legislator parties

key_findings.finding: Candidate positioning and district vote share: the author replicates Ansolabehere, Snyder and Stewart (2001) with non-incumbent estimates. Midpoint positioning matters, but its effect is shrinking. The text reports the effect as about 4 points in 1996, falling to 1.96 in the 2000s, but the table coefficients do not reproduce these figures (see limitations).

Non-incumbent measures cover presidential and other federal candidates. 369 presidential candidates are recovered, including third parties. In the 2012 Republican field, pro-life donor share ranks Santorum highest, while Romney and Huntsman draw more pro-choice donor money.
key_findings.numbers: 369 presidential candidates; NPAT response rate 64% (532 of 830) in 1996, down to about one-third recently (PDF p.27)

key_findings.finding: Donor ideology sorts by industry and occupation. Academics, entertainment, newspaper and print media, and online computer services skew left. Oil, gas and coal is the most reliably conservative, followed by agriculture, mining and construction.
key_findings.numbers: Mean contributor point for each left-aligned industry lies left of the mean Democratic candidate

key_findings.finding: Non-incumbent measures address the question of who is missing from polarization accounts. The author argues that the disappearance of moderates through attrition is only part of the story, and that office-seekers must be modeled alongside office-holders.

limitations: Author states that CFscores are not the 'true' ideology measure, that roll-call and contribution measures are expected to differ, and that perfect correspondence is neither expected nor desirable (PDF p.12).
Strategic giving may bias estimates. The author reports covariate effects at the margins and argues the bias is small, but does not rule it out (PDF pp.21-22; supplement).

Party-driven classification: CFscores classify moderates who overlap the opposing party poorly; the classification gap to DW-NOMINATE narrows for close votes but not lopsided votes (supplement, 'Roll Call Classification, cont.').

Contribution Accounting Assumption: CA cannot control non-spatial covariates such as incumbency or committee assignments; the IRT count model can, but it is computationally infeasible at full scale (PDF pp.7-8).

Cross-state bridging depends on the assumption that donors hold the same ideal point when giving to state and federal candidates; the author calls it 'unheroic and verifiable' but does not test it directly beyond the 0.88 and 0.93 correlations (PDF p.24 fn 13).

Record linkage errors. Corporate board members were the training set: 57% were assigned a single ID; 42% were split (type 1, information loss); 13% failed the 90% threshold. Two type-2 errors merged different people (family members at the same employer), and type 2 errors can bias estimates (supplement, Record Linkage; PDF p.51). Disclosure of address and occupation is weaker in the 1980s and early 1990s.

Sample restrictions drive results: individual gifts to labor, corporate and trade PACs are dropped; corporate and trade PACs are excluded from estimation because of mixed motives; candidates need 2+ contributors and contributors need 2+ recipients; period-specific scores need 25+ contributors per cycle (PDF pp.9-10, 15).
Assumption: fixed legislator ideal points in the polarization trends exclude ideological adaptation, so the trends capture replacement but not adaptation (PDF p.30 fn 15).
Presidential nominees: joint fundraising after nomination shifts estimates, so the author uses pre-nomination scores as more accurate (supplement; PDF p.47).
Pro-life share interpretation is ambiguous: the author says it could reflect economic dimension dominance or the limits of stated positions (PDF pp.32-33).

Internal inconsistencies to check before citing: (a) abstract says over 100 million records, the data section says over 103 million; (b) the text says a 0.28-unit (two SD) shift gives about 4 points in 1996 and falls to 1.96 points in the 2000s, but Table 3 gives midpoint coefficients of 7.44 and 1.71 for those periods, and 0.28 x 7.44 is about 2.1, not 4; the 2000s column is labeled 2002-2010 in the table; (c) the text says investor and ideological models are on par for corporate PACs, but unconstrained investor log-lik (-1,687,949) beats ideological (-1,694,458) in Table 2; (d) a supplement table caption reads 'replicates Table ??' (unresolved cross-reference), and the Table 3 supplement caption says House while its title says Senate.
Reproducibility: the identity-resolution software and database access are available only on request; the CFscore data and code are promised as a public database (PDF p.57).
measures: Common-space CFscores (candidates, contributors, PACs, state and federal), on a standardized scale (weighted mean 0, SD 1 of contribution amounts)
Period-specific CFscores (Nokken-Poole style) and incumbent vs non-incumbent CFscores
DW-NOMINATE (common-space, 1-112th Congress) and Turbo-ADA / Turbo-CCUS interest-group scores
Percent of votes correctly classified and APRE (cutting-line procedure)
Money-weighted standard deviation of contributor allocation (McCarty, Poole and Rosenthal 2006); 0.577 is the random-giving benchmark
Pro-life share of donor money y_j = prolife / (prolife + prochoice)
Deviance residual RDev (Cameron and Windmeijer 1996) and log-likelihood for strategic-giving model comparison
NPAT candidate-survey scores (Ansolabehere, Snyder and Stewart 2001) for state and congressional validation

rel.summary_md:
Bonica (SSRN draft, 2013) estimates common-space ideal points (CFscores) for candidates and donors. The data are more than 100 million federal and state contribution records from 1979 to 2012, and the method is correspondence analysis on a contributor-by-recipient matrix. Donors who give in both state and federal races bridge the two levels. Pooled across parties, candidate CFscores track DW-NOMINATE at r = 0.92 (unstratified). Within party the correlation is much weaker: 0.56 to 0.72. Scores for non-incumbents predict their later roll-call scores about as well as incumbent scores do.

For this system, the important result is the test of why people give. On 5,000 individual donors with 25 or more federal gifts (2004-2012), the ideological model beats both the partisan electoral model and the investor model by log-likelihood. The investor model barely beats the baseline. For corporate and trade PACs the investor model is competitive, and in its unconstrained form it fits better than the ideological model (Table 2). That is why those PACs are left out of estimation.

Three consequences follow:
1. The paper does not show that dollars buy more in competitive seats. The partisan electoral model, which Paul highlighted, loses to the ideological model for individual donors.
2. CU and bank PAC money is exactly the mixed-motive class. Because individual donors give by ideology, money and stance are entangled, so any test of whether money moves members needs an ideology control.
3. The record-linkage appendix gives Mentat's identity ladder a concrete error profile. When merges went wrong, they joined family members at the same employer.

The paper measures who gives and why. It does not test whether giving changes votes or buys access, so it cannot calibrate any money-response constant.

bearings.paper_claim: Partisan electoral model (donors fund competitive races to shift seat share) fits worse than the ideological model for individual donors: log-lik partisan -1,405,855 vs ideological -1,334,200 (5,000 donors with 25+ federal gifts, 2004-2012). Competitive-seat covariates shift candidate CFscores only 0.03-0.05 (about 1/20 SD). The paper models donor allocation; it never estimates the effect of a dollar on the recipient.
bearings.paper_location: Table 2, PDF p.21; text PDF pp.19-22; supplement Tables 1-3
bearings.system_side: c = 1 + 1.0*exp(-max(lean,0)/5.0) scales effective dollars on both money legs. The code comment calls AMPLITUDE and SCALE uncalibrated owner judgment, with reciprocity NOT validated (D-104..D-108).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Does not carry over as support. Bonica's dependent variable is where donors send money, not how much access or alignment a dollar buys in a competitive seat. Even if competitive races drew more money, c is a claim about dollar efficacy, not allocation. The sample is individuals from 2004-2012; corporate PACs were tested separately and found mixed-motive. The evidence neither supports nor calibrates c.

bearings.paper_claim: Individuals give mainly on ideology (investor -1,504,601 vs baseline -1,520,312; ideological -1,334,200). For corporate and trade PACs (N=1,312) the investor model is competitive: unconstrained investor -1,687,949 beats ideological -1,694,458. This is why such PACs are excluded from scaling.
bearings.system_side: pflip = a/(a+b), with a saturating term on CU PAC money and b on bank+finserv PAC money relative to receipts. Money is the minority partner (WM 0.35 / WP 0.65), justified in the code as 'money buys access/effort > votes'.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Both money legs are corporate or trade-association PAC money, the class Bonica finds mixed-motive. So his ideology result for individuals cannot be borrowed to say these dollars are purely expressive. The ideological-giving result also implies selection: allied money flows to already-aligned members. Any validation of the money term (the question about roll-call alignment after controlling for party) is confounded unless it controls for an ideology measure such as CFscore or DW-NOMINATE. The paper says nothing about vote-buying or access effects, so WM, HALFF and MAXSHIFT get no calibration from it.

bearings.paper_claim: The main testable implication of the partisan electoral model is that donors fund competitive races. It loses to the ideological model for individuals: partisan -1,405,855 vs ideological -1,334,200.
bearings.system_side: Defend and contest plays scale value by comp = 1 - Ballotpedia security. They assume CU money matters more where the seat is less safe.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Paul's highlight (donors direct funds to competitive races) states the hypothesis the paper rejects for individuals, not a finding. It describes donor behavior, not the payoff of a play. It neither supports nor refutes the comp weighting.

bearings.paper_claim: Of 49,418 individuals with 25+ contributions, only 167 (0.3%) exceed the 0.577 random-giving benchmark. Mean money-weighted SD of recipient ideology is 0.20. Donors overwhelmingly fund ideologically proximate candidates.
bearings.system_side: F1 gate: members whose overall tier is Skeptic, Highly Skeptical or Opponent get zero money in every allocator, so money funds allies rather than trying to convert opponents.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Descriptive support only. Bonica shows ideological donors already behave the way the gate requires, so the gate matches observed practice. It does not show that funding opponents fails to convert them. Window: individual donors 2004-2012; PAC behavior differs (Table 2).

bearings.paper_claim: Identity resolution trained on corporate board members: 57% assigned a single ID, 42% split across IDs (information loss), 13% below the 90% threshold. The two type-2 errors (wrong merges) joined family members at the same employer. Address and occupation disclosure is weaker before the mid-1990s.
bearings.system_side: Ordered ladder. Exact name + same zip returns AUTO unless the employer contradicts the company, which downgrades to HIGH. A suffix mismatch returns REVIEW. There is no name-frequency weighting.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Bonica's known false-merge mode (same surname and household, same employer) is exactly where Mentat's AUTO rule cannot tell people apart when a Jr/Sr suffix is missing from one record: same name, same zip, no employer contradiction. His split-rate figures suggest that Mentat's conservative ladder trades recall for precision, as his did. The figures come from his probabilistic linker, not from Mentat's rules, so they are a reference point, not an estimate of Mentat's error rate.

bearings.paper_claim: Corporate and trade PACs are mixed-motive: the unconstrained investor model fits as well as or better than the ideological model (-1,687,949 vs -1,694,458), while individuals and labor PACs are ideological (labor: ideological -231,022 vs investor -252,936).
bearings.system_side: SEATS-W regresses the weekly Democratic share of industry giving on the prior week's change in expected Democratic House seats: -3.47 pp per seat, block bootstrap p .0086-.0174, one election (2022); Senate null.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Consistent: strategic re-allocation is the behavior Bonica's model comparison allows for corporate and trade PACs but not for individuals. His tests are cross-sectional over 2004-2012 and use static covariates (incumbency, majority status, competitiveness), not within-cycle forecast movement. The 2022 result is one election and stays UNVERIFIED until reproduced by another path. If the SEATS-W giving series mixes individual employee gifts with PAC money, Bonica predicts the individual part dilutes the strategic signal.

gaps_exposed: No ideology covariate anywhere in the money or influence chain. Validation questions (flip-model, demographic pillar, CFPB isolation) control only for party. Bonica shows party drives the pooled r = 0.92, while within-party correlation is 0.56-0.72, and that donors select on ideology. Any test that money or stance predicts CU alignment needs a CFscore or DW-NOMINATE control, or it measures selection.

The flip model and money response treat CU and industry PAC dollars as exogenous pressure. Bonica's ideological-giving result implies the reverse direction (ideology causes money), which the model never addresses or tests.

Electoral plays and the contest route have no position estimate for challengers or open-seat candidates. Bonica's non-incumbent CFscores (r = 0.96 with later incumbent scores) are the standard way to place them, and they are publicly available as DIME.

Mentat's identity ladder has no name-frequency weighting and no documented false-merge rate. Bonica's linkage appendix shows that same-employer family members are the main false-merge mode, which an exact-name + zip AUTO rule does not guard against.
flags: Paul's positions list Bonica 2013 (partisan electoral model) as grounding for competitiveness-multiplier and electoral-plays. The paper tests that model and finds it fits worse than the ideological model for individual donors (Table 2). It is also about donor allocation, not dollar efficacy. Do not cite it as support for c. Reciprocity stays NOT validated (D-104..D-108).
The pooled CFscore vs DW-NOMINATE r = 0.92 runs across the party fault line. Quote it as UNSTRATIFIED, or give strata: House D 0.56 / R 0.66, Senate D 0.64 / R 0.72; window 96th-112th Congresses.

Paper-internal inconsistencies: the text says investor and ideological models are on par for corporate PACs, but Table 2 has the unconstrained investor ahead. The Table 3 midpoint effects (7.44 and 1.71) do not reproduce the text's '4 points' and '1.96'. Cite table values, not prose.

Paul's p.7 margin note asks for a short-term theory of engagement and sunk costs. The paper's model is static spatial allocation with a cost function on the total given. It offers no dynamic engagement or sunk-cost mechanism, so the note is an open extension, not something the paper supplies.
Avoid access or influence language when citing this paper. It tests and largely rejects investor (access) motives for individuals and does not measure access.
rel.paul_alignment: Partly aligned. Paul's highlights capture the main claim correctly: individuals give on ideology, and corporate or interest-group PACs weigh other considerations. The flip model's conservative 'money buys access, not votes' framing is compatible with that, though Bonica tests why donors give, not what money buys. Paul's use of the paper for competitiveness and electoral plays is a misreading: the highlighted line (donors fund competitive races) states the partisan electoral model's prediction, which the paper's evidence rejects for individuals. The stance-money gate and the SEATS-W result fit his reading better than c does. His p.7 margin note (short-term engagement, sunk costs) is still unaddressed by both the paper and the system. The annotation record lists the 2014 AJPS citation with no takeaways, so his notes do not reflect the later competitiveness rulings (D-104..D-108).

related.why: Later Bonica work drawing on the same contributor-ID and CFscore database (DIME) to study donors.
DW-NOMINATE is the roll-call benchmark CFscores are validated against (r = 0.92 pooled, Table 1 classification).
A field experiment on whether contributions buy access, the outcome Bonica's motive test does not measure. Together they separate why donors give from what giving buys.
Strategic, investor-type donor behavior and graph-based donor identity resolution. It contrasts with Bonica's ideological-individual finding and parallels his linkage approach.
Low overlap between PAC giving and lobbying fits Bonica's finding that much giving is ideological rather than investment.
